Chapter 3. Control Structures and Array Data
In a specific context, using the appropriate statement makes the program clearer, more legible, and more reliable. According to programming conventions in several earlier languages and based on the specific characteristics of each statement, loop statements are often used in specific contexts as follows:
• FOR is often used in loops where the number of iterations is known in advance, meaning that the loop is usually organized in the form of one (or more) counter variables running from a certain value and stopping when reaching another predetermined value. For example, the common form of the for statement is as follows:
• for (i = gt1 ; i <= gt2 ; i++) … meaning i increases from gt1 to gt2, or
• for (i = gt2 ; i >= gt1 ; i--) … meaning i decreases from gt2 down to gt1
• In contrast to FOR, WHILE and DO … WHILE are often used in loops where the number of iterations is not known in advance; they are often used when repeating or stopping depends on a logical expression.
• WHILE is used when there is a possibility that the loop body will not execute even once, that is, if the loop condition is false right from the start, whereas DO … WHILE is used when we know for sure that the loop block must be executed at least once.
III. DATA ARRAYS
1. One-dimensional array
a. Meaning
When we need to store a sequence of n data elements, we need to declare n corresponding variables with n different names. This will be very difficult for programmers to remember and manage all the variables, especially when n is large. In practice, we obviously encounter a lot of data that are related to each other in some aspect; for example, they are of the same type and represent the same object: such as the coordinates of a vector, the elements of a matrix, the students of a class, or the text lines of a document... Taking advantage of this characteristic, all data (of the same type and describing the same object) can share a single name to distinguish them from other objects, and to distinguish data within the same object, we use index numbers for them; from there, managing variables will be easier, and the program will be neater and more systematic.
Suppose we have 2 vectors in three-dimensional space, each vector needs 3 variables to store 3 coordinates, so to store the coordinates of 2 vectors, we have to use 6 variables, for example, x1, y1, z1 for the first vector and x2, y2, z2 for the second vector. When referring to a specific component of the array, we use the array name along with the

b. Declaration
<type_name> <array_name>[number_of_components] ;   // uninitialized
<type_name> <array_name>[number_of_components] = { value_sequence } ;   // initialized
<type_name> <array_name>[ ] = { value_sequence } ;   // initialized
− The type name is the data type of the components; these components have the same
type. Occasionally, we also refer to components as elements.
− The above declaration syntax is similar to declaring a normal variable name, but with the addition of the number of
components in the array between a pair of square brackets [], which is also called the
size of the array. Each array name is a variable, and to distinguish it from ordinary variables,
it is also called an array variable.
− An array of data is stored in memory as a sequence of contiguous cells. The
number of cells equals the number of components of the array, and the length (in bytes) of each cell is sufficient to
hold the information of each component. The first cell is indexed by 0, the next cell
by 1, and so on until the end. Thus, if an array has n components, the last
cell in the array will be numbered n - 1.

with each value separated by a comma (,); these values will be assigned respectively to
the elements of the array starting from the 0-th element to the end of the sequence. The number of values can
be less than the number of elements. Array elements that have not been given a value will remain undefined
until they are assigned a value in the program.

2. Character Strings 
A character string is an arbitrary sequence of characters (including spaces); therefore, it can be stored using an array of characters. However, in order for the machine to recognize this character array as a string, a terminating character is required, conventionally the character with code 0 (i.e. '\0') at some position in the array. In that case, the string is the sequence of characters starting from the first element (the 0-th) up to the first null terminator (excluding the remaining characters in the array). 
0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7 
H   E   L   L   O   \0 
H   E   L   \0   L   O   \0 
\0   H   E   L   L   O   \0 
The figure above illustrates 3 strings, each stored in a character array of maximum length 8. The content of the first string is "Hello", with an actual length of 5 characters, occupying 6 cells in the array (including the cell containing the terminating character '\0'). The second string has content "Hel" with length 3 (occupying 4 cells), and the last string represents an empty string (occupying 1 cell). Note that the character array is declared with length 8, but the strings may only occupy a certain number of characters in this array, up to at most 7 characters. 
a. Declaration 
char <string_name>[length];   // uninitialized 
char <string_name>[length] = string;   // initialized 
char <string_name>[] = string;   // initialized 
− The array length is the maximum number of characters that can be in the string. The actual length of the string is counted only from the beginning of the array up to the string terminator (excluding the null terminator ‘\0’). 
− Since a string must have a null terminator, when declaring the array length, one extra element must be declared. In essence, the maximum length of the string = array length - 1. For example, to declare an array s that can hold a string of maximum length 80 characters, we must declare char s[81]. 
− The second declaration method includes string initialization, which is a sequence of characters placed between double quotes. For example: 
char hoten[26];   // full name string containing at most 25 characters

b. Usage
Similar to other data arrays, character strings have the characteristics of arrays; however,
they also have differences. Below are these similarities and differences.
• Accessing a character in a string: the syntax is identical to an array. Example:
char s[50] = "I\'m a student" ;   // note the character ' ph ả i   đượ c vi ế t là \'
cout << s[0] ;   // in kí t ự   đầ u tiên, t ứ c kí t ự   'I' 
s[1] = 'a' ;   // reset the 2-th character to 'a'
• You must not perform direct operations on strings such as:
char s[20] = "Hello", t[20] ;   // declare two strings s and t
t = "Hello" ;   // incorrect, can only be assigned during declaration
t = s ;   // incorrect, cannot assign an entire array
if (s < t) …   // incorrect, cannot compare two arrays
…
• The input operator >> can still be used, but with many limitations. For example,
char s[60] ; 
cin >> s ; 
cout << s ; 
if the input string is, for example, "Tin h ọ c hoá", the >> operator only reads "Tin" into s
(discarding all characters following the whitespace); therefore, when printed to the screen, only the word "Tin" is displayed.
Because operations cannot be directly applied to strings, compilers
provide pre-written library functions declared in the prototype file string.h. These
functions solve most tasks that require string manipulation. They provide users with
means to manipulate strings such as assigning, comparing, copying, calculating string length, inputting, printing,
etc. To use these functions, the beginning of the program must include string.h. Most
of these functions will be introduced in the following section.

Because the input operator >> has limitations with character strings, C++ provides a dedicated function (also
g ọ i là ph ươ ng th ứ c)   cin.getline(s,n)   để   nh ậ p xâu kí t ự . Hàm có 2   đố i v ớ i s là xâu c ầ n
to input content and n-1 is the maximum number of characters of the string. Similar to the character input method
cin.get(c), khi g ặ p hàm cin.getline(s,n) ch ươ ng trình s ẽ   nhìn vào b ộ   đệ m bàn phím l ấ y
extracts n-1 characters (if enough, or takes all remaining characters, except the Enter character) and assigns them to s. If at
that moment the buffer is empty, the program will pause and wait for the user to enter data (a sequence of
characters) from the keyboard. The user can enter a sequence of arbitrary length until pressing
Enter; the program will take the first n-1 characters and assign them to s, while the remaining part is still stored
in the buffer (including the Enter character) to be used for the next input. Obviously, after assigning the
characters to s, the program will automatically place the null terminator character into the next slot of string s.
Example 1: Consider the following code snippet
char s[10] ; 
cin.getline(s, 10) ;

second, the user does not need to enter more data; the program automatically takes the rest of the remaining data
(because it is not up to 9 characters) "0abcd" to assign to s. Then it prints to the screen. Thus, on the screen

d.   M ộ t s ố   hàm x ử   lí xâu (#include <string.h>) 
•   strcpy(s, t) ; 
Assign the content of string t to string s (replacing the assignment operator =, which is not allowed). The function
will copy the entire content of string t (including the null-terminating character) into string s. To
use this function, it is necessary to ensure that the length of array s is at least equal to the length of array t.
Otherwise, the null-terminating character will not be written into s, and this
may cause the system/program to freeze when running.
Example:
char s[10], t[10] ; 
t = "Face" ;   // not allowed
s = t ;   // not allowed
strcpy(t, "Face") ;   // allowed, assigns "Face" to t
strcpy(s, t) ;   // allowed, copies t to s
cout << s << " to " << t ;   // in ra: Face to Face 
•   strncpy(s, t, n) ; 
Copies n characters from t into s. This function only performs the copying task and does not automatically
append the null-terminating character to s. Therefore, the user must add a statement to place character '\0' at the end of string
s after copying is completed.
Example:
char s[10], t[10] = "Steven"; 
strncpy(s, t, 5) ;   // copy 5 characters "Steve" into s
s[5] = '\0' ;   // set the null terminator
// print sentence: Steve is young brother of Steven
cout << s << " is young brother of " << t ; 
A useful application of this function is to copy an arbitrary substring of t and place it into s. For
example, to copy a substring of length 2 characters starting from the 3-th character of string t and place it into s, we write
strncpy(s, t+3, 2) . In addition, the copied substring can be placed at any position in s
(not necessarily from the beginning of string s); for instance, to place it starting from the 5-th position, we write:
strncpy(s+5, t+3, 2) . This statement means: take 2 characters, the 3-th and the 4-th of string t, and place them
into 2 cells, the 5-th and the 6-th of array s. Based on this, we can write code snippets

−   In the declaration, it can also be initialized with a sequence of row values, rows
separated by commas, each row enclosed in a pair of curly braces {}, and all
initialization values enclosed within a pair of curly braces {}.

•   Similar to a one-dimensional array, the dimensions in the array are also numbered starting from 0. 
•   Operations on the entire array are not used; instead, they must be performed on
each element of the array. 
•   To access an element of the array, we use the array name accompanied by 2 indices indicating the row
and column position of the element. These indices can be real expressions, in which case
C++ will automatically cast them to integers.

−   Declare 2 matrices of 4 rows and 5 columns A, B containing integers: 
int A[3][4], B[3][4] ; 
−   Declaration with initialization: 
int A[3][4] = { {1,2,3,4}, {3,2,1,4}, {0,1,1,0} }; 
With this initialization, we have the matrix: 
1   2   3   4 
3   2   1   4 
0   1   1   0 
where: A[0][0] = 1, A[0][1] = 2, A[1][0] = 3, A[2][3] = 0 …

Example 4: Trim spaces 2 of string s. The program uses variable i running from the beginning of the string 
to the first position containing a non-space character. From this position, copy each remaining character of 
the string back to the beginning of the string by using an additional variable j as an index for the new string. When copying 
finishes, j will be at the end of the (new) string. Let j run backward toward the beginning of the string until encountering the 
first non-space character. Place the string terminator here. 
main() 
{ 
char s[100]; 
cin.getline(s, 100);   // nh ậ p xâu s 
int i, j ; 
i = j = 0; 
while (s[i++] == ' '); i-- ;   // skip the leading spaces 
while (s[i] != '\0') s[j++] = s[i++] ;   // copy the remaining part into s 
while (s[--j] == ' ') ;   // skip the trailing spaces 
s[j+1] = '\0' ;   // place the string terminator 
cout << s ; 
} 
Example 5: Run a circular marquee text from right to left in the middle of the screen. 
Suppose 30 characters of the marquee string are displayed. We use a loop. Cut the first 30 characters 
of the string into variable hien, and display this variable on the screen. The next iteration cuts 30 
characters of the string but shifted to the right by 1 characters, puts them into variable hien, and displays it on the screen. The 
process continues; in each iteration, we shift the content to be displayed on the screen by 1 characters, and due to 
the visual effect of the eyes, we see the text running from the right edge to the left edge of the screen. To 
make the process run circularly (when reaching the last character of the string, it will wrap around and display from the 
first character of the string), the program uses variable i to mark the starting point of the substring to be cut 
into hien; when i equals the length of the string, the program resets i = 0 (cutting again from the beginning of the string). In 
addition, to join the end of the string with the beginning (forming a circle) right from the start of the program, 
the marquee string is doubled.

CHAPTER 4 
FUNCTIONS AND PROGRAMS 
Pointers and address arithmetic 
Functions

I. POINTERS AND ADDRESS ARITHMETIC 
Before discussing functions and programs, in this section we will talk about a
new kind of variable called pointer, its meaning, purpose, and how to use it. Pointer
variables are a powerful feature of C++; they allow us to directly access memory
to handle difficult problems using just a few simple program statements. This
also contributes to making C++ a language close to low-level languages
such as assembly. However, because of their simplicity and conciseness, using pointers requires
high caution and rich experience from the programmer. 
1. Address, the & operator 
Before running, every program must allocate the variables declared by the user somewhere
in memory. To facilitate easy access back to these variables, memory
is numbered; each byte corresponds to an integer, called the address of that byte,
from 0 to the end of memory. From there, each variable (with its variable name) is associated with an integer which is the address
of the first byte allocated to that variable. The number of bytes allocated to a variable
varies (but placed consecutively from low to high) depending on the data type of the variable (and
depending on the concept of each programming language); however, just by knowing the variable name or the address
of the variable, we can read/write data to/from those variables. Therefore, in addition to using the variable
name, we can also use their address to access their content. In
short, variables, memory cells, and addresses are closely related. C++ provides a unary
operator & to get the address of variables (except array variables and character strings). If x is a
variable, then &x is the address of x. Hence, the following statement tells us where x is located in
memory: 
int x ; 
cout << &x ;   //   đị a ch ỉ   s ẽ   đượ c hi ệ n d ướ i d ạ ng c ơ   s ố   16. Ví d ụ   0xfff4

Chapter 4. Functions and programs 
For array variables, the array name is itself the address of the array, so there is no need
to use the & operator. For example, the address of array a is a (not &a). On the other hand, the
address of array a is also the address of the first byte occupied by array a, and it is also
the address of the first element of array a. Therefore, the address of array a is the address
of element a[0], which is &a[0]. In summary, the address of array a is a or &a[0]. 
In summary, remember: 
int x;   // declare integer variable x 
long y;   // declare long integer variable y 
cout << &x << &y;   // in   đị a ch ỉ   các bi ế n x, y 
char s[9];   // declare character array s 
cout << a;   // in   đị a ch ỉ   m ả ng s 
cout << &a[0];   // in   đị a ch ỉ   m ả ng s (t ứ c   đị a ch ỉ   s[0]) 
cout << &a[2];   // in   đị a ch ỉ   kí t ự   s[2] 
The following figure illustrates some variables and their addresses in memory. 
200   201   500   501   502   503   650   651   …   …   658 
1   2   4   3   2   1   H   E   L   L   O   \0 
x   y   s 
Variable x occupies 2 bytes of memory and has the address 200; variable y has the address 500 and occupies 4 bytes
of memory. String s occupies 9 bytes of memory at address 650. The memory bytes of a variable are contiguous. 
Operations related to addresses are called address arithmetic. However, we
are still not allowed to directly manipulate addresses, such as placing a variable at this or
that address (this task is handled by the compiler), or adding/subtracting two addresses
with each other is meaningless... Permitted operations on addresses must still go through
intermediate variables storing addresses, called pointer variables. 
2.   Pointers 
a.   Meaning 
−   A pointer is a variable that stores the address of another variable. If p is a pointer storing the address
of variable x, we say p points to x and x is pointed to by p. Through the pointer, we can
work with the content of the memory locations that p points to. 
−   For pointer p to point to x, we must assign the address of x to p.

Chapter 4. Functions and Programs
− To work with the addresses of variables, it is necessary to use pointer variables that point to those variables.
b. Declaring pointer variables
<ki ể u   đượ c tr ỏ > <*tên bi ế n> ; 
The address of a variable is the address of the first memory byte of that variable. Therefore, to retrieve the content of a variable, the pointer must know the number of bytes of the variable, that is, the type of the variable that the pointer will point to. This type is also called the pointer's type. Thus, declaring a pointer variable is similar to declaring a normal variable, except that an asterisk * must be added before the variable name (or after the type name). Example:
int *p ;   // declare variable p as a pointer variable pointing to integer data type.
float *q, *r ;   // two float pointers q and r.
c. Using pointers, the * operator
• To make pointer p point to variable x, we must use the assignment p = address of x.
− If x is not an array, we write: p = &x.
− If x is an array, we write: p = x or p = &x[0].
• Do not assign p to a specific address constant. For example, writing p = 200 is incorrect.
• The * operator allows retrieving the content of the location that p points to; for example, to assign the content of the location pointed to by p to variable f, we write f = *p.
• & and * are 2 inverse operations. Specifically, if p = &x then x = *p. From that, if p points to x, then wherever x appears can be replaced by *p and vice versa.
Example 1 :
int i, j ;   // declare 2 integer variables i, j
int *p, *q ;   // declare 2 integer pointers p, q
p = &i;   // make p point to i
q = &j;   // make q point to j
cout << &i ;   // h ỏ i   đị a ch ỉ   bi ế n i 
cout << q ;   // h ỏ i   đị a ch ỉ   bi ế n j (thông qua q) 
i = 2;   // assign i equal to 2
*q = 5;   // assign j equal to 5 (via q)
i++ ; cout << i ;   // t ă ng i và h ỏ i i, i = 3

3.   Operations with pointers 
Above, we have presented 2 unary operations related to addresses and pointers, which are & and *. In this section, we continue to consider other operations that work with pointers. 
a.   Assignment operation 
−   Gán con tr ỏ   v ớ i   đị a ch ỉ   m ộ t bi ế n: p = &x ; 
−   Assigning a pointer to another pointer: p = q; (after this assignment operation, p and q contain the same address, pointing to the same location). 
Example 2: 
int i = 10 ;   // declare and initialize variable i = 10 
int *p, *q, *r ;   // declare 3 integer pointers p, q, r 
p = q = r = &i ;   // all point to i 
*p = q**q + 2**r + 1 ;   // i = 10*10 + 2*10 + 1 
cout << i ;   // 121 
b.   Address increment and decrement operations 
p ± n: the pointer pointing to the n-th element after (before) p. 
One unit of pointer increment/decrement is equal to the size of the pointed-to variable. For example, suppose p is an integer pointer (2 bytes) pointing to the address 200, then p+1 is the pointer pointing to the address 202. Similarly, p + 5 is the pointer pointing to the address 210. p − 3 contains the address 194. 
194   195   196   197   198   199   200   201   202 
p   −   3   p   p + 1 
Thus, pointer increment and decrement operations allow convenient work on arrays.
If a pointer is pointing to an array (that is, containing the first address of the array), incrementing the pointer by 1 unit will shift the pointer to point to the second element, ... From there, we can let the pointer iterate from the beginning to the end of the array by incrementing the pointer by one unit each time, as in the for loop below.

(*p)++ ;   // post-increment the value pointed to by p ≡ increment a[0] to 4 
++(*p) ;   // pre-increment the value pointed to by p ≡ increment a[0] to 4 
*(p++) ;   // dereference p (3) and increment pointer p (post-increment), p → a[1] 
*(++p) ;   // increment pointer p (pre-increment), p → a[1] and dereference p (7) 
Note: 
• Distinguish between p+1 and p++ (or ++p): 
• p+1 is considered a different pointer from p. p+1 points to the element after p. 
• p++ is the pointer p itself but pointing to a different element. p++ points to the element after
the element p initially pointed to. 
• Distinguish between *(p++) and *(++p): 
Auto-increment and auto-decrement operators are also unary; their precedence is higher than
other binary operators and higher than the dereference operator (*). Specifically: 
*p++   ≡   *(p++) 
*++p   ≡   *(++p) 
++*p   ≡   ++(*p) 
Just like with integer variables, combining these operators can easily lead to
confusion; therefore, parentheses should be used to specify the order of evaluation.

a[i] = *(a+i). 
Note that when writing *(p+1) = *(a+1), we see that the roles of p and a in this expression are
the same, both accessing the value of the element a[1]. However, writing *(p++) is
different from *(a++), specifically writing p++ is valid while a++ is not allowed. The reason is that although p
and a both represent the address of the array a, p is actually a variable, its value can be changed,
while a is a constant, its value is not allowed to change. For example, writing x = 3 and
then increasing x by x++ is possible, but writing x = 3++ is not possible. 
Example 1: Print the entire array via a pointer. 
int a[5] = {1,2,3,4,5}, *p, i; 
1: p = a; for (i=1; i<=5; i++) cout << *(p+i);   // p không thay   đổ i 
or: 
2: for (p=a; p<=a+4; p++) cout << *p ;   // thay   đổ i p 
In option 1, the pointer p does not change during the execution of the
for statement; to access the i-th element of the array a, we use the syntax *(p+i). 
For option 2, the pointer will move along the array a starting from the address a
(the first element) to the last element. At the i-th step, p will point to the element a[i], so
we only need to print the value *p. To check when p reaches the last element, we can
compare p with the address of the end of the array, which is the starting address of the array plus the number of elements in a
and minus 1 (i.e., a+4 in the above example). 
b. Pointers and character strings 
A character pointer can be considered as a string variable, in which the string is all
the characters starting from the byte pointed to by the pointer up to the first encountered byte '\0'. Therefore, we can
declare strings in the form of character pointers as follows. 
char *s ; 
char *s = "Hello" ; 
String functions can still be used just as when we declare it in the form of a character array.
In addition, unlike character arrays, we are allowed to use assignment for 2 strings in pointer
form, for example: 
char *s, *t = "Tin h ọ c" ; s = t;   // thay cho hàm strcpy(s, t) ; 
Essentially, the above assignment is just assigning 2 pointers to each other; it allows s to now
also point to where t points (i.e., the character sequence "Tin h ọ c" already allocated in memory). 
When declaring a string in pointer form, it does not yet have specific memory, so usually
accompanying the declaration, we need to request memory allocation for the string with the required length. For example: 
char *s = new char[30], *t ;

II. FUNCTIONS 
A function is a subprogram within a larger program. A function receives (or does not receive)
arguments and returns (or does not return) a value to the calling program. In the case
where it does not return a value, the function acts like a procedure in other programming languages. A
program is a collection of functions, among which there is a main function named main(); when running
the program, the main() function will be executed first and will call other functions. The termination of the
main() function is also the termination of the program. 
Functions help divide the program into separate modules that operate
independently of the semantics of the larger program, meaning a function can be used
in this program and can also be used in another program, making it easy
to test and maintain the program. Functions have several characteristics: 
•   Located inside or outside the source file containing the program that calls the function. A source
file can contain multiple functions, 
•   Called from the main program (main), from another function, or from itself (recursion
), 
•   Cannot be nested. 
•   There are 3 ways to pass values: Pass by value, pass by reference, and pass by pointer. 
1.   Function Declaration and Definition 
a.   Declaration 
A function typically performs the function of: calculating based on arguments and returning a result
value, or simply executing some specific task without returning a calculation
result. Usually, the type of the return value is called the type of the function. Functions are usually
declared at the beginning of the program. Predefined functions are declared in files
nguyên m ẫ u *.h. Do   đ ó,   để   s ử   d ụ ng   đượ c các hàm này, c ầ n có ch ỉ   th ị   #include <*.h>   ở

c.   Notes on function declaration and definition 
•   The parameter list in a function declaration may or may not contain parameter names; usually,
we only declare the parameter types without needing to declare the parameter names, whereas in
the first line of the function definition, full parameter names must be present. 
•   The end of a function declaration must have a semicolon (;), whereas the end of the first line
of a function definition does not have a semicolon. 
•   A function may have no parameters (an empty parameter list); however, the parentheses following
the function name must still be written. For example: clrscr(), lamtho(), vietgiaotrinh(), … 
•   A function may not need to be declared if it is defined before any
function calls it. For example, one can write the main() function first (in the program
text), and only afterward write functions "con". Since the main() function
will certainly call these subfunctions, their list must be declared
before the main() function. Conversely, if the subfunctions are written (defined)
first, there is no need to declare them anymore (because the definition already
implies the declaration). This rule applies to any two functions A and B,
not just the main() function, meaning that if B calls A, then before that, A must be defined
or at least have a declaration line for A. 
2.   Function calls and function usage 
A function call is allowed to appear in any expression, statement of another function,
… If a function call lies within that very function itself, we call it recursion. To call
a function, we only need to write the function name and the list of specific values passed to the parameters enclosed in
parentheses ().

all occurrences of a formal parameter will be assigned the specific value
of the corresponding actual argument in the list; after that, the function proceeds to execute
the statements of the function (to compute the result). 
−   The actual argument list passed to the formal parameters has the same number of elements
as the number of parameters in the function and is passed to the parameters in the corresponding order. The
actual arguments can be constants, variables, or expressions. Variables in the values

3. Functions with Default Arguments 
This section and the next section discuss several practical extensions of C++ over C related to functions, namely functions with default arguments and how to create and use functions that share the same name. Another important extension is passing arguments by reference, which will be discussed together in the section on passing actual arguments to functions. 
In the previous part, we affirmed that the number of actual arguments must equal the number of formal parameters when calling a function. However, in practice, a function is very often called with the values of some formal parameters being repeated over and over. In such cases, always having to write a long list of identical actual arguments for each call is an uninteresting task. From this reality, C++ introduces a new function syntax such that a list of actual arguments in a call does not necessarily have to be fully written if some of them already have predetermined values. This syntax is called functions with default arguments and is declared with the following syntax: 
<ki ể u hàm> <tên hàm>( đ 1, …,   đ n,   đ m đ 1 = gt1, …,   đ m đ m = gtm) ; 
− The arguments đ1, …, đn and default arguments đmđ1, …, đmđm are all declared as before, meaning they consist of the argument type and argument name. 
− Specifically, the default arguments đmđ1, …, đmđm are assigned additional default values gt1, …, gtm. Any call to this function must have all actual arguments corresponding to đ1, …, đm, but may or may not have actual arguments corresponding to the default arguments đmđ1, …, đmđm. If an argument does not have an actual argument, it will automatically be assigned the declared default value. 
Example 5: 
− Consider the function xmh(int n = 100), in which n defaults to 100, meaning that if xmh(99) is called, the screen is cleared 99 times, whereas if xmh(100) or more concisely xmh() is called, the program will clear the screen 100 time(s). 
− Similarly, consider the function int luythua(float x, int n = 2); This function has one default parameter which is the exponent n; if the function call omits this exponent, the program understands it as computing the square of x (n = 2). For example, the call luythua(4, 3) is understood as 4 3

5:   double max(double a, double b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
And a function call of any form such as max(3,5), max(3.0,5), max('O', 'K') is satisfied. We can raise the question: with all 5 functions having the same name like that, which function does the program call? The problem is easily resolved because the program will rely on the types of the arguments when calling to decide which function to run. For example, the call max(3,5) has 2 arguments both of integer type, so the program will call function 1, the call max(3.0,5) targets function number 2, and similarly the program will run function number 3 when encountering the call max('O','K'). Thus, a characteristic of functions with the same name is that in their argument list, there must be at least one pair of arguments that have different types. Another distinguishing characteristic via arguments is that the number of arguments in the functions must be different (if their types are the same). 
For example, drawing shapes: straight lines, triangles, squares, rectangles on the screen is similar; they only depend on the number of connecting points and their coordinates. Therefore, we can declare and define the 4 drawing functions mentioned above with the same name. For instance: 
void ve(Diem A, Diem B) ;   // draw line segment AB 
void ve(Diem A, Diem B, Diem C) ;   // draw triangle ABC 
void ve(Diem A, Diem B, Diem C, Diem D) ;   // draw quadrilateral ABCD 
in the above example, we assume Diem is a data type storing the coordinates of points on the screen. The function ve(Diem A, Diem B, Diem C, Diem D) will draw a square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, or trapezoid depending on the coordinates of the 4 points ABCD; generally, it is used to draw an arbitrary quadrilateral. 
In summary, multiple functions can be overloaded (with the same name) if they satisfy the following conditions: 
•   The number of arguments in the functions is different, or 
•   The types of the arguments in the functions are different. 
This name overloading technique also applies to operators. In the object-oriented programming section, we will see that users are allowed to define new operators while still using old names such as +, -, *, / … 
5.   Variables, reference arguments 
A variable can be assigned a new alias, and then wherever the variable appears, it is equivalent to using the alias and vice versa. Such an alias is called a reference variable; its practical meaning is to allow "tham chi ế u" to another variable of the same type, that is, using another variable but via the name of the reference variable. 
Like normal variable declaration, however, we add an ampersand (&) before the variable name. We can temporarily distinguish 3 types: normal variables with normal names, pointer variables with an * symbol before the name, and reference variables with an & symbol.

<ki ể u bi ế n> &<tên bi ế n tham chi ế u> = <tên bi ế n   đượ c tham chi ế u>; 
This declaration syntax allows us to create a new reference variable and make it refer to the referenced variable (of the same type and must be declared beforehand). In this case, the reference variable is also called an alias of the referenced variable. Note that there is no syntax to declare only the name of a reference variable without initialization. 
Example: 
int hung, dung ;   // declare integer variables hung, dung 
int &ti = hung;   // declare reference variables ti, teo referring to 
int &teo = dung;   // hung dung. ti, teo are aliases of hung, dung 
From this point onward, using the names hung, ti or dung, teo is equivalent. 
Example: 
hung = 2 ; 
ti ++;   // t ươ ng   đươ ng hung ++; 
cout << hung << ti ;   // 3 3 
teo = ti + hung ;   // equivalent to dung = hung + hung 
dung ++ ;   // equivalent to teo ++ 
cout << dung << teo ;   // 7 7 
So what is the purpose of using additional reference variables? 
The internal organization of a reference variable differs from a normal variable in that its content is the address of the variable it represents (similar to a pointer variable). For example, the statement 
cout << teo ;   // 7 
prints the value 7, but in fact this is not the content of variable teo; the content of teo is the address of dung. When teo needs to be printed, the program will refer to dung and print the content of dung (7). Other operations on teo behave similarly (for example, teo++), which in reality increments the content of dung by one (rather than that of teo). From the organization of reference variables, we see that they are like pointers, but more convenient in that when accessing the value of the referenced variable (dung), we only need to write the name of the reference variable (teo) without having to prepend the dereference operator (*) as in the case of using pointers. This difference is useful when passing arguments to functions with the purpose of modifying the content of external variables. This concept is presented more clearly in section 6 of this chapter. 
Note: 
•   A reference variable must be initialized upon declaration.

4. Declaring overloaded functions 
Functions with the same name are also known as overloaded functions. This is a technique that allows using
the same name for "gi ố ng nhau" functions (same purpose) but operating on
different data types or on different amounts of data. For example, the following function finds the maximum
of 2 integers: 
int max(int a, int b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
If we set c = max(3, 5), we will have c = 5. However, similarly, if we set c =
max(3.0, 5.0), the program will produce an error because the (float) values do not match the (int) type
of the arguments in the max function. In such a case, we must write a new function to calculate
the max of 2 real numbers. The purpose and operation of this function are completely identical to the previous function,
however, in C and other classic programming languages, we are forced to use a new name
for this "m ớ i" function. For example: 
float fmax(float a, float b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
Similarly, for convenience, we will write additional functions: 
char cmax(char a, char b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
long lmax(long a, long b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
double dmax(double a, double b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
In summary, we will have 5 functions: max, cmax, fmax, lmax, dmax; using names like that
will cause inconvenience when needing to call the function. C++ allows us to declare and define all 5 functions
above with the same 1 name, for example, max. Then we have 5 functions: 
1:   int max(int a, int b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
2:   float max(float a, float b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
3:   char max(char a, char b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; } 
4:   long max(long a, long b) { return (a > b) ? a: b ; }

Chapter 4. Functions and Programs 
•   Although similar to pointers, pointer operations cannot be used on reference variables. In general, they should only be used when passing arguments to functions. 
6.   Methods of Passing Arguments 
There are 3 ways to pass actual arguments to formal parameters in a function call. Among them, the method we have used up to now is called pass-by-value, meaning that the formal parameters will receive specific values from the function call, perform calculations, and then return a value. To easily understand argument passing methods, we will examine how the program works with arguments when executing a function. 
a.   Pass-by-value 
Let us reconsider the example function luythua(float x, int n) computing x n . Suppose that in the main program, we have variables a, b, f holding the values a = 2, b = 3, and f has no value yet. To compute a b and assign the computed value to f, we can call f = luythua(a,b). When encountering this call, the program will organize it as follows: 
−   Create 2 new variables (i.e., 2 memory cells in memory) named x and n. Assign the contents of these memory cells to the values in the call, that is, assign 2 (a) to x and 3 (b) to n. 
−   Upon reaching the declaration section (of the function), the program creates additional memory cells named kq and i. 
−   Perform the calculation (assign the result to kq). 
−   Finally, take the result in kq and assign it to the memory cell f (which is an existing memory cell declared beforehand outside the function). 
−   End the function and return to the calling program. Since the function luythua has finished its calculation, the memory cells created during the function's execution (x, n, kq, i) will be deleted from memory. The calculation result is preserved in the memory cell f (not deleted because it has nothing to do with the function). 
The above is the usual way of passing arguments. The question arises: suppose that besides computing f, we also want to modify the values of the memory cells a, b (when passing them to the function), can this be done? To solve this problem, we need to follow a different technique, through the role of pointer and reference variables. 
b.   Pass-by-pointer 
Consider the example of swapping the values of 2 variables. This is a small requirement, but it is encountered many times in programs, for example, to sort a list. Therefore, it is necessary to write a function to perform the above requirement. The function returns no result. Since the variables that need to be swapped are not known in advance at the time of writing the function, we must pass them into the function as arguments, meaning the function has two arguments x, y representing the variables whose values will change later.

And the last thing the program does after finishing the function execution is to delete these new variables. Chapter 4. Functions and Programs
Thus, the swap function needs to be rewritten so that the change of values is not performed on temporary variables, but is actually performed on external variables. To do so, instead of passing the values of external variables to arguments, we will now pass their addresses to arguments, and changes will have to be performed on the content of these addresses. That is the reason why we must use pointers as parameters instead of normal variables. Specifically, the swap function is rewritten as follows:
void swap(int *p, int *q)
{
int t;   // declare temporary variable t
t = *p ;   // set the value of t to the content of the location p points to
*p = *q ;   // replace the content of the location p points to with the content of the location q points to
*q = t ;   // replace the content of the location q points to with the content of t
}
With such a function organization, clearly if we let p point to variable x and q point to variable y, the swap function will actually change the content of x, y, not of p, q.
From that, the function call will be swap(&x, &y) (meaning passing the address of x to p, p points to x, and similarly q points to y).
Thus, 3 characteristics can be summarized for writing a function that changes external variable values as follows:
• The function's arguments must be pointers (for example, int *p)
• Operations related to this argument (in the function body) must be performed at the location it points to (for example, *p = …)
• The function call must pass the address to p (for example, &x).
In addition to the swap function presented, here we provide an additional example to see the necessity of having a function that allows modifying external variables. For example, the function to solve a quadratic (degree 2) equation is very commonly encountered in scientific and engineering problems. That is, given 3 numbers a, b, c as 3 coefficients of the equation, it is required to find 2 its roots x1, x2. One cannot take the return value of the function as the roots because there is only 1 return value while we need up to 2 roots. Therefore, we need to declare 2 variables "ngoài" in the program to store the roots, and the function must modify these 2 variables (meaning to store the solved root values). Thus, the function to be written needs to have 5 arguments, in which 3 arguments a, b, c represent the coefficients, which do not change, and 2 variables x1, x2 represent the roots; these 2 arguments must be declared as pointers. In addition, the equation may have no real roots, 1 root, or 2 roots, so the function will return the value as the number of roots of the equation; in the case of 1 root (a double root), the root value will be assigned to x1.

Chapter 4. Functions and Programs 
c. Pass by reference 
A function written with reference parameters is much simpler than with pointer parameters and is similar to the normal way of writing (pass by value), with the only difference being that the parameters are declared as references. 
To compare 2 usages, let us recall the points to note when writing functions with pointers: 
− The function parameter must be a pointer (e.g., int *p) 
− Operations related to this parameter in the function body must be performed at the location it points to (e.g., *p = …) 
− The function call must pass an address to p (e.g., &x). 
Let us compare this with reference parameters, specifically: 
• The function parameter must be a reference (e.g., int &p) 
• Operations related to this parameter must be performed at the location it points to, meaning the address to operate on. Since an operation on a reference variable is essentially an operation on the variable it references, in the function you only need to write p in all operations (instead of *p as with pointers) 
• The function call must pass an address to p. Since p itself, when referencing a variable, will contain the address of that variable, the function call only needs to specify the variable name, e.g., x (instead of &x as with pointers). 
In summary, for functions written with references, the only change is in the parameters (which are references), while everywhere else is written simply as in pass-by-value. 
Example 7: Swap the values of 2 variables 
void swap(int &x, int &y) 
{ 
int t = x; x = y; y = t; 
} 
and the function call is also as simple as in pass-by-value. For example: 
int a = 5, b = 3; 
swap(a, b); 
cout << a << b;

For 2-dimensional arrays, declaring parameters as well as function calls is much more complex than for

−   Declare according to the true nature of the 2-dimensional array float x[m][n] specified by C++,
meaning x is a 1-dimensional array of m elements, each element of which has type float[n]. From that, 
the parameter is declared as a formal 1-dimensional array (no need for the number of elements - here
is the number of rows) of type float[n]. That means it can be declared as follows: 
float x[][n] ;   // array with unspecified number of elements, each element is n numbers 
float (*x)[n] ;   // a pointer whose type is an array of n numbers (float[n]) 
To access element i, j, we still use the syntax x[i][j]. The name of
array a is written normally in the function call. In general, according to this declaration method,
accessing is simple, but the method also has a limitation: the number of columns of the array
passed to the function must be fixed to n. 
−   Consider the array float x[m][n] actually as a one-dimensional array float x[m*n] and use
the declaration method as in a one-dimensional array, that is using a pointer float *p to
access each element of the array. This method has a limitation in the call: 
the address passed to the function is not array a, but needs to be cast to (float*)
(to match p). With this method, let k be the index of element a[i][j] in the
one-dimensional array (m*n), we have the relationship between k, i, j as follows: 
•   k = *(p + i*n + j) 
•   i = k/n

Chapter 4. Functions and programs 
in memory and can be accessed through its name or its address. In order to 
access (call the function) via its address, we must declare a pointer storing this address 
and then call the function by calling the pointer's name. 
a. Declaration 
<ki ể u giá tr ị > (*tên bi ế n hàm)(d/s tham   đố i); 
<ki ể u giá tr ị > (*tên bi ế n hàm)(d/s tham   đố i) = <tên hàm>; 
We see that the syntax for declaring a function pointer is also similar to declaring a variable pointer (simply 
placing an * before the name); in addition, *function_name must be enclosed within a pair of parentheses (). For example: 
−   float (*f)(int);   // declares a function pointer named f pointing to a function 
// having one argument of type int and returning a value of type float. 
−   void (*f)(float, int);   // a pointer pointing to a function with a pair of arguments (float, int). 
or more complex: 
−   char* (*m[10])(int, char) // declares an array of 10 function pointers pointing to 
// functions with a pair of arguments (int, char), the return 
// value of these functions being a character string. 
Note: distinguish between the 2 declarations: float (*f)(int) and float *f(int). The former declaration 
declares a function pointer named f. The latter declaration can be rewritten as float* f(int), which 
declares a function f whose return value is a float pointer. 
b. Initialization 
A function pointer is also like other pointers, allowed to be initialized upon declaration 
or assigned to a specific function address after declaration. Just like array 
data types, the function name itself is an address constant pointing to itself. Therefore, the syntax of initialization 
as well as assignment is as follows: 
bi ế n con tr ỏ   hàm = tên hàm; 
where f and the pointed function name must have the same return type and argument list. 
In other words, in order to use the pointer f to point to a certain function (or family of functions), f must 
be declared with the same return type and argument list as that function. For example: 
float luythua(float, int);   // declaration of the power function 
float (*f)(float, int);   // declaration of pointer f compatible with function luythua 
f = luythua;   // make f point to the power function

Chapter 4. Functions and Programs 
• For variables that have a clear shared nature (especially large-sized variables) which multiple functions use for the same purpose, they should be declared as external (global) variables. This saves time for the programmer because they do not have to declare them multiple times in multiple functions, saves memory because they do not have to be created temporarily each time the functions run, and saves program execution time because there is no need to organize memory to store and release them. For example, in the student management program (Chapter 6), student variables are shared and consistent in most functions (view, delete, edit, add, statistics...), so they can be declared as external variables; this also increases the consistency of the program (all student variables are the same for all subfunctions of the program). 
In summary, the most general principle is to try to create functions independently and self-contained, unaffected by other functions and not affecting the operation of other functions as much as possible. 
2. Variables with special purposes 
a. Constant variables and the const keyword 
To use constants, the keyword const can be declared before the variable declaration. The scope and lifetime are the same as variables, meaning constant variables can also be local or global. Constant variables must always be initialized beforehand. 
The keyword const can be declared before formal parameters to disallow modifying the values of external variables (especially for arrays and character strings, because these variables themselves are treated as pointers, so the function could otherwise modify the values of the external variables passed to it). 
The following example shows that constants can also be declared in different scopes: 
const int MAX = 30;   // global 
void vidu(const int *p)   // local 
{ 
const MAX = 10;   // local 
… 
} 
void main() 
{ 
const MAX = 5;   // local

b. Static variables and the static keyword 
Declared using the static keyword. It is a local variable but still retains its value after
exiting the function. Its scope is like a local variable, meaning it can only be used in
the function where it is declared. However, its lifetime is considered like a global variable, meaning after
the function finishes executing, the variable still exists and still retains its value after exiting the function. This
value continues to be used when the function is called again, which means a static variable is only initialized
once during the first function call. If not initialized, C++ automatically assigns the value
0 (default = 0). For example:

Looking at the main() function, we see that the value 2 3 is calculated by setting x = 2, i = 3 and calling
the function luythua(x,i). The desired result displayed on the screen would be the value 8; however,
this is not the case. Before printing this result to the screen, the function xmh() was called 
to clear the screen. This function uses an external variable i as its counter variable in
a for loop, and after exiting the for loop (which is also the end of xmh()), i takes the value 6. This external
variable i is then used in the call luythua(x,i) of the main() function, meaning at this
point x = 2 and i = 6, and the result printed to the screen will be 2 6 = 64 instead of 8 as expected. 
In summary, " đ i ể m y ế u" leading to the error in the above program lies in the fact that the programmer 
"tranh th ủ " used the variable i for 2 functions xmh() and main() (by declaring it as an
external variable) but for different purposes. Consequently, after xmh() finishes executing, i
is changed to a value different from the value of i initially initialized. To fix the bug in the above
program, we need to redeclare the variable i: either declare an additional i in main() (which will shadow the external variable
i), or have a variable i in both xmh() and main() (local to each function). 
From that, we should establish several programming principles so that we can avoid
such undesirable bugs: 
•   if a variable is used only for the internal purpose of a function, it should be declared
as a local variable within that function. For example, loop counter variables: normally
they are used even exclusively within the loop itself, not even for the entire
function; therefore, they should not be declared as external
variables. When the function terminates, these local variables also terminate,
without affecting any other function. Another advantageous feature of
local declarations is that they make the function self-contained and independent of any
other function or program. For example, the function xmh() could be ported to run in
another program without any modification if i had been declared inside
the function. Whereas in this example, although the function xmh() still works, in
another program, if i does not exist as an external variable (for xmh() to use), the
function will cause an error.

Allows including the contents of other existing files into the program before compilation. The files that need to be included in the program are usually those containing prototype declarations of constants, variables, functions, etc., available in C, or functions written by the programmer. There are two forms of writing this directive. 
1: #include <t ệ p> 
2: #include “ đườ ng d ẫ n\t ệ p” 
The declaration form 1 allows C++ by default to look for the file in a predetermined directory (declared via the Options\Directories menu), usually the TC\INCLUDE directory, and the files are prototype files of the C++ library. 
The declaration form 2 allows searching for the file by path; if there is no path, it will look in the current directory. The files are usually files (libraries) created by the programmer and placed in the same directory containing the program. This syntax allows the programmer to divide a program into multiple modules placed in several different files for easier management. It is especially useful when the programmer wants to create their own libraries.

In addition to the fact that the directive #define allows replacing macro_name with any arbitrary character string, it
can also be written in a parameterized form (with arguments). For example, to find the maximum of 2 numbers, instead of having
to write multiple max functions (each corresponding to a different numeric type), now we only need
to replace them with a simple parameterized macro as follows: 
#define max(A,B) ((A) > (B) ? (A): (B)) 
then in the program, if there is a line x = max(a, b), it will be replaced by: x =
((a) > (b) ? (a): (b)) 
Note: 
•   The macro name must be written immediately adjacent to the parentheses of the argument list. For example, do not
write max   (A,B). 
•   #define bp(x) (x*x) is written incorrectly because bp(5) is correct, but bp(a+b) will become (a+b*a+b)
(that is, a+b+ab). 
•   Similarly, writing #define max(A,B) (A > B ? A: B) is incorrect (?), so always
enclose arguments in parentheses. 
•   #define bp(x) ((x)*(x)) is written correctly, but suppose a programmer wants to calculate
the square of 2 using the following code snippet: 
int i = 1; 
cout << bp(++i);   // 6 
then the printed result will be 6 instead of the correct result 4. The reason lies in the fact that the compiler
will replace bp(++i) with ((++i)*(++i)), and with i = 1, the program will execute as 2*3 = 6.
Therefore, be careful when using auto-increment/decrement operators in parameterized macros.
In general, one should limit the use of complex macros, as they can cause side
effects that are difficult to control.

Chapter 5. Structure and Union Data Types 
CHAPTER 5 
STRUCTURE AND UNION DATA TYPES 
Structure type 
Self-referential structures and linked lists 
Union type 
Enumeration type 
To store values consisting of multiple identical data components, we have the array variable type. In reality, a lot of data is a collection of different data types gathered together; to manage this kind of data, C++ provides the structure data type. An example of structure-type data is a resume / profile record in which each employee is stored in a table consisting of multiple different data types such as full name, age, gender, salary, etc. 
I. STRUCTURE TYPE 
1. Declaration, initialization 
To create a structure type, the user needs to declare the name of the type (which is a user-defined identifier), along with the names of the data components contained in this structure type. A structure type is declared according to the following template: 
struct <type name> 
{ 
các thành ph ầ n ; 
} <danh sách bi ế n>; 
− Each component is like an individual variable of the type; it consists of a type and a component name. A component is also called a field. 
− The structure type name part and the variable list part may or may not be present. However, in the declaration, the final terminating character must be a semicolon (;). 
− Structure types are allowed to be nested, meaning that a component of a structure type can itself be a field of a structure type. 
− A variable of structure type will be allocated memory such that its components are arranged contiguously in the order of their appearance in the declaration.

cout << p[10].hoten ;   // in h ọ   tên sinh viên th ứ   10 
cout << (p+10)   →   gt ;   // in gi ớ i tính c ủ a sinh viên th ứ   10

Note: The precedence of the member access operator (dot) is higher than that of the address-of operator (&) and dereference operator (*), so parentheses must be written properly. 
b. Address of structure members 
Members of a structure are just like variables; therefore, obtaining the address of these members is also similar to ordinary variables. For example, the address of member gioitinh of structure variable x is &x.gt (note that the precedence of . is higher than &, so &x.gt is equivalent to &(x.gt)), the address of field hoten of the 10-th element in array lop is lop[10].hoten (hoten is a character string), similarly the address of member diem of the variable pointed to by p is &(p -> diem). 
Example: 
struct Sinhvien { 
char hoten[25] ; 
Ngaythang ns; 
int gt; 
float diem ; 
} lop[60], *p, x = { "NVA", {1,1,1980}, 1, 9.0) }; 
lop[10] = x; p = &lop[10] ;   // p points to the 10-th student in lop 
char *ht; int *gt; float *d;   // pointers to member types 
ht = x.ht ;   // let ht point to member hoten of x 
gt = &(lop[10].gt) ;   // gt points to gt of the 10-th student 
d = &(p -> diem) ;   // d points to diem of the student that p points to

2. Concept of linked lists 
A linked list is a data structure that allows representing and managing a list
using structures linked together through pointers within the structures. There are many forms of
linked lists depending on the connections, for example: 
−   Singly linked list, where each structure contains a pointer pointing to the next
or preceding structure. For a list with pointers pointing backward, the first structure
of the list will point to the pointer constant NULL, and the last structure is marked
by the pointer last pointing to this structure. For a list with pointers pointing
to the next structure, the first structure is marked by the pointer head and the last
structure contains a NULL pointer. 
−   Doubly linked list consisting of 2 pointers, one pointing to the preceding structure and one pointing
to the succeeding structure, with 2 ends of the list marked by the pointers head,
last. 
−   Circular linked list consisting of 1 pointer pointing forward (or backward), where the two ends of the
list are connected to form a circle. Only one pointer head is needed to
mark the head of the list. 
Since the structure contains pointers pointing to the next structure and/or the preceding
structure, from one structure we can access another structure

3. Operations on linked lists
Below we briefly describe how to perform some operations on a singly
linked list.
a. Creating a new element
To create a new element, we usually follow these steps:
− use the new operator to allocate a memory area sufficient to hold an element of the
list.
− enter the information to be stored into the new element. The pointer tiep is set to
NULL.
− attach the newly created element to the list. There are two ways:
• either attach it to the beginning of the list, in which case the position of the head pointer (pointing to the beginning of the
list) is adjusted to point to the new element.
• or attach it to the end of the list by having the tiep pointer of the last element of
the list (currently pointing to NULL) point to the new element. If the list has a
last pointer pointing to the end of the list, last is adjusted to point to the
new element. If the list does not have a last pointer, to find the last
element the program must traverse from the beginning, starting from the head pointer until
reaching the element pointing to NULL, which is the last element of the list.

c. Traversing the list 
Traversal is the operation of going through each element of the list; at each element, the program performs some action on that element, which we call visiting that element. A visit operation can simply be displaying the information content of that element on the screen, for example. 
To traverse the list, we only need to have a pointer p run from the beginning to the end of the list until the last element has the pointer tiep = NULL, then stop. The statement to move pointer p to its next element is: 
p = p   →   tiep ; 
d. Searching 
Given a list in which each element contains a field called a key field, usually of a primitive type or a combination of several such fields. The problem posed is to find in the list an element whose key field value is equal to a given value. The process of performing this task is essentially also a traversal problem, in which the operation "th ă m" is comparing the key field of the element with the given value; if they match, we print the result and stop. If the entire list has been traversed and no element has a key field matching the given value, the list is considered not to contain this value.

IV. ENUMERATION TYPE
Consecutive integer values (starting from 0) can be assigned to specific names using the enumeration type according to the following declaration:
enum tên_ki ể u { d/s tên các giá tr ị   }; 
Example:
enum Bool {false, true}; 
declares a new type named Bool that only takes 1 of 2 named values false and true, where false corresponds to the value 0 and true corresponds to the value 1. The above enum type declaration is also equivalent to the following series of macros:
#define false 0
#define true 1
With the Bool type, we can declare some variables as follows:
Bool Ok, found; 
the two variables Ok and found will only take 1 of 2 values false (instead of 0) or true (instead of 1). This means one can assign:
Ok = true; 
ho ặ c:   found = false; 
However, integer values cannot be directly assigned to enum variables; instead, it must be done through type casting. Example:
Ok = 0; // incorrect
Ok = Bool(0) ; // correct
or Ok = false ; // correct

I. GRAPHICS 
1. Graphics concepts 
a. Pixels and resolution 
A screen in graphics mode is a set of picture points (pixel - picture elements). The number of pixels and their horizontal and vertical arrangement on the screen is called resolution. Therefore, the resolution is usually characterized by a pair of numbers indicating the number of pixels horizontally and vertically on the screen. For example, a VGA monitor in mode 2 has a resolution of 640x480, meaning that on each horizontal line of the screen 640 pixels can be drawn, and on each vertical column 480 pixels can be drawn. The columns and rows are numbered from 0, from left to right (for columns) and from top to bottom (for rows). A picture point, also known as a pixel, is the intersection of a column and a row on the screen, and its position is represented by a coordinate pair (x, y) where x represents the column and y represents the row. For example, with the monitor above, the "first" pixel located at the top-left corner of the screen has coordinates (0,0) and the "last" point at the bottom-right corner has coordinates (639,479). The point with coordinates (150,200) is the intersection of the 150-th column and the 200-th row. 
b. Graphics driver 
There are many different types of graphics screens. Each type of screen requires a corresponding driver. C provides screen drivers in the BGI directory located under the root directory of C (TC or BC), including: 
Driver name Graphics screen type 
ATT.BGI ATT & T6300 (400 lines) 
CGA.BGI IBM CGA, MCGA, and compatible machines 
EGAVGA.BGI IBM EGA, VGA, and compatible machines

c. Adjusting text justification 
In each direction (horizontal or vertical), there are 3 text justifications corresponding to the following constants: 
1. Horizontally: 
LEFT_TEXT = 0 : Write from left to right.

5. Movement 
Principle: erase the shape at the old position and then redraw that shape at the new position along the direction of motion. To erase, we redraw the shape at the exact same old position but with a color matching the background color (hence the drawn shape blends into the background as if it has been erased). To know the current background color, one can use the function setcolor(getbkcolor()). In summary, the following scheme can be given: 
− redraw the shape with the background color at the old position // erase the shape 
− delay // pause 
− redraw the shape (with the shape's color) at the new position // shape moves to another position 
If the above steps are repeated, we will see the shape moving from one position to another. 
For complex shapes, to erase quickly, we can redraw the shape in XOR_PUT mode as described in the next section.

• setviewport(x1, y1, x2, y2, clip) : Creates a new window in graphics mode.
The coordinates of the points will then be recalculated according to this new window. Specifically, the point
(x1, y1) of the screen will now be calculated with the new coordinates (0,0). If
clip = 0, drawings are allowed to extend beyond the window frame; if clip =
1, the parts of the drawing outside the window frame will be clipped. 
• getviewsettings(struct viewporttype *vp) : Retrieves the current window coordinates into
the pointer variable vp. The window type is a structure as follows: 
struct viewporttype {int left, top, right, bottom, clip;}; 
• imagesize(x1, y1, x2, y2) : Returns the size (in bytes) of a bitmap image within
the rectangular frame defined by the coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2). 
• getimage(x1, y1, x2, y2, *pict) : Saves an image from the screen into the memory area
pointed to by the pointer pict. 
• putimage(x1, y1, *pict, op) : Writes the image saved at the location of pointer
pict to the screen. op is the mode specifying how the image is displayed on the screen; the colors of the points
will be determined by the color of the image saved in pict and the current color
of the point on the screen. These two colors will "tr ộ n" according to the operations defined

6. Plotting graphs of mathematical functions 
To plot the graph of a mathematical function, we plot each point of the graph one by one. Each point is determined by a coordinate pair (x, y) on the screen. Therefore, it is necessary to compute these points in screen coordinates. The steps to follow include: 
• Determine the coordinate system. Usually, we take the center of the screen as the origin of the coordinate system by redefining the screen viewport using the command: 
viewport(midx, midy, maxx, maxy, 0); 
where midx, midy are the coordinates of the center of the screen, and maxx, maxy are the coordinates of the bottom-right corner of the screen. The above command creates a viewport that is the bottom-right quarter of the screen. The last parameter (1) allows drawings to be drawn outside of this viewport border. Thus, the center of the screen becomes the origin of the coordinate system. The coordinates of the center of the screen are now considered as (0,0). 
• Determine the scale: It is necessary to determine how many pixels on the screen's x and y axes correspond to one unit of x and y of the function to be plotted. Because the number of pixels along the width and height of the screen is different, and because the value of the function (y) can be very large compared to the argument (x) (for example, the function y = x 4) or very small (for example, the function y = sinx), these scales along x and y may be different so that the drawing on the screen looks balanced. Determining these scales depends on experience and is usually adjusted after running the program for testing. 
• Draw the coordinate axes: The coordinate axes may or may not be drawn. The following function allows drawing the coordinate axes with the origin located at the center of the screen. 
void vetruc() // Draw coordinate axes 
{ 
line(0, midy, maxx, midy); // horizontal axis 
line(maxx-7, midy-3, maxx, midy); // arrow 
line(maxx-7, midy+3, maxx, midy); 
line(midx, 0, midx, maxy); // vertical axis 
line(midx-3, 7, midx, 0); // arrow 
line(midx+3, 7, midx, 0); 
outtextxy(midx+6, midy+6, "(0, 0)"); // print coordinate (0,0) 
}

I. STRUCTURED PROGRAMMING AND OBJECT-ORIENTED PROGRAMMING 
1. Structured programming methodology 
− Structured programming organizes a program into subprograms.
In some languages such as PASCAL, there are 2 types of subprograms: procedures and functions, while in C++ there is only one type of subprogram: functions. 
− A function is an independent program unit used to perform a specific task such as: entering data, printing results, or performing some computational tasks. A function requires arguments and local variables/arrays for its private use. 
− Data exchange between functions is carried out via arguments and global variables. 
− A structured program consists of data structures (such as variables, arrays, records) and functions, procedures. 
− The primary task of organizing structured program design is organizing the program into functions and procedures. 
For example, consider the following requirement: Write a program to input the coordinates ( x,y ) of a sequence of points, then find a pair of points that are furthest apart from each other.

1. Class Declaration 
To declare a class, we use the keyword class as follows: 
class class_name

// Declaration of methods (functions)

Note: Declaring a class does not occupy memory; only objects of the
class actually occupy memory. 
Attributes of a class can be variables, arrays, pointers of standard types (int, float,
char, char*, long, ...) or predefined non-standard types (structures, unions,
classes, ...). An attribute of a class cannot have the type of that class itself, but it can be a
pointer to this class, for example: 
class A 
{ 
A x;   // Not allowed, because x has type class A 
A* p ;   // Allowed, because p is a pointer of type class A 
} ; 
2. Declaration of Class Members (Attributes and Methods) 
a. Keywords private and public 
When declaring data members and methods, you can use the keywords
private and public to specify the access scope of these members. Among them, the
keyword private specifies that members (declared with this keyword) can only be used
inside the class (within the bodies of the class's methods). Functions outside the class
(which are not methods of the class) are not allowed to use these members. 
This feature demonstrates information hiding inside the class; to access
this information, it is necessary to go through the member functions of that class. Therefore,
the information has high integrity, and the processing of this information (data) is more
consistent, and almost all data in classes are declared with this keyword.
In contrast to private, members declared with the keyword public are allowed
to be used both inside and outside the class; this allows the program to
use these functions to access the class data. Obviously, if the data
members are declared as private, then the member functions must have at least a few

b. Using constructors in declarations 
+ Once constructors are defined, we can use them in declarations to create an object and simultaneously initialize the attributes of the created object. Based on the arguments in the declaration, the compiler will know which constructor needs to be called. 
+ When declaring an object variable, arguments can be used to initialize the attributes of the object variable. 
+ When declaring an array of objects, using arguments for initialization is not allowed. 
+ A statement declaring an object variable will call the constructor 1 time. 
+ A statement declaring an array of n objects will call the constructor n times. 
Example: 
DIEM_DH d;   // Calls the parameterless constructor. 
// Result: d.x = 0, d.y = 0, d.m = 1 
DIEM_DH u(300, 100, 5);   // Calls the parameterized constructor. 
// Result: u.x = 300, u.y = 100, d.m = 5 
DIEM_DH v(400, 200);   // Calls the parameterized constructor. 
// Result: v.x = 400, v.y = 200, d.m = 15 
DIEM_DH p[20] ;   // Calls the parameterless constructor 20 times 
Note: For functions with parameters of class types, the arguments are only considered formal parameters; therefore, declaring the arguments (in the function header) will not create a new object and consequently will not call the constructors. 
c. Using constructors in memory allocation 
+ When allocating memory for an object, arguments can be used to initialize the attributes of the object, for example: 
DIEM_DH *q = new DIEM_DH(40, 20, 4);   // Calls the parameterized constructor 
// Result: q   →   x = 40, q   →   y = 20, q   →   m = 4 
DIEM_DH *r = new DIEM_DH ;   // Calls the parameterless constructor 
// Result: r   →   x = 0, r   →   y = 0, r   →   m = 1 
+ When allocating memory for a sequence of objects, using arguments for initialization is not allowed, for example: 
int n = 30; 
DIEM_DH *s = new DlEM_DH[n] ;   // Calls the parameterless constructor 30 times.

a. Default Copy Constructor 
Suppose a certain class has been defined, for example class PS (fraction). Then: 
+ We can use declaration statements or memory allocation to create new objects,
for example: 
PS p1, p2 ; 
PS *p = new PS ; 
+ We can also use a declaration statement to create a new object from an
existing object, for example: 
PS u; 
PS v(u) ; // Create v from u 
The meaning of this statement is as follows: 
− If the class PS does not define a copy constructor yet, this statement will call
a default copy constructor (of C++). This function will copy the bit-by-bit
content of u into the corresponding bits of v. Thus, the memory areas
of u and v will have the same content. Obviously, in most cases,
if the class does not have pointer- or reference-type attributes, using
the default copy constructor (to create a new object with content
identical to a given object) is sufficient, and there is no need to implement a new copy
constructor. 
− If the class PS already has a copy constructor (the syntax will be discussed later), the
statement: PS v(u); will create a new object v, then call the copy constructor to
initialize v from u.

V. DESTRUCTOR 
A destructor is a member function of a class (method) that has the opposite function of a constructor. A destructor is called before releasing (deleting) an object to perform some ''cleanup'' tasks before the object is destroyed, for example, freeing a memory region managed by the object, removing the object from the screen if it is currently displayed, ... 
Destroying an object usually occurs in the following 2 cases: 
+ In operators and functions that free memory, such as delete, free, ... 
+ Releasing local variables and arrays when exiting a function or method. 
1. Default Destructor 
If a destructor is not defined in a class, a default destructor that does nothing is generated. For many classes, the default destructor is sufficient, and there is no need to introduce a new destructor. 
2. Rules for Writing Destructors 
Each class has only one destructor written according to the following rules: 
+ Function type: Like a constructor, a destructor has no type and no return value. 
+ Function name: The name of the destructor consists of a tilde (placed in front) and the class name: 
~Class_name 
+ Arguments: A destructor has no arguments

3. The role of the destructor in class DT 
In the previous section, the definition of class DT (polynomial) was quite complete, including: 
+ Constructors 
+ Stream extraction >> and insertion << operators 
+ Operator functions performing operations +, -, *, / 
However, a destructor is still missing to deallocate the memory managed by the DT object (to be destroyed). 
Let us analyze the flaws of this program: 
+ When the program calls an operator method to perform polynomial addition, subtraction, or multiplication, an intermediate object is created. A memory block is allocated and assigned to this intermediate object to manage. 
+ When the calculation is finished and the method exits, the intermediate object is destroyed; however, only the memory for the attributes of this object is freed. Meanwhile, the memory block (containing the coefficients of the polynomial) managed by the intermediate object is not freed at all. Thus, the amount of wasted memory will increase. 
The above disadvantage is easily overcome by adding to class DT the destructor mentioned in section 3 above.
